Question: Can you provide an example of a transitional fossil found in a natural environment?
Answer: There are four very famous ones. One of the very first transitional fossils discovered was archeopteryx - a transition between non-avian dinosaurs and birds. Archaeopteryx had many features of non-avian theropod dinosaurs, such as teeth and a long bony tail. It also had features of birds such as wings and asymmetrical feathers, although it lacked the bony breastbone that anchors the flight muscles of modern birds. The Archaeopteryx fossils have been found in the Solnhofen Limestone, a stratum originating in fine sticky carbonate muds in a lagoon environment in what is now northern Germany. The fine mud has preserved the fossils in exquisite detail. A second example of a clearly transitional fossil is Tiktaalik, transitional between lobe finned fish and land-based trilobites. Tiktaalik had scales and gills like a fish, but it also had a triangular, flattened head and unusual, cleaver-shaped fins. Its fins had thin ray bones for paddling like most fish, but they also had sturdy interior bones that would have allowed Tiktaalik to prop itself up in shallow water and use its limbs for support as most four-legged animals do. Those fins and other mixed characteristics mark Tiktaalik as a crucial transition fossil, a link in evolution from swimming fish to four-legged vertebrates. The Tiktaalik fossils were found in the upper Devonian Fram Formation on Ellesmere Island in Canada. Ther Fram formation was laid down by river sediments at a time when this area was close to the equator. The fine sediments and rapid deposition led to preservation of the fossil remains. The third example is Pakicetus, a transitional link between land-based mammals and whales. Whalelike features were an upward-facing eye placement and a thickened skull bone known as the auditory bulla, which was specialized for underwater hearing. But Pakicetus still had four legs. It likely waded in water, sometimes close to fully submerged. Pakicetus was found in the Eocene red continental beds of the Kuldana formation in Pakistan. The Kuldana formation has preserved other fossil specimens of early whale species. The fourth example is the famous australopithecine fossil known as “Lucy”. Lucy had a small skull akin to that of non-hominin apes, but clearly walked bipedal and upright, akin to that of humans. Lucy was found in the Hadar formation in Ethiopia and is dated at 3.7 million years ago. The region's rocks consist mainly of mudstones, siltstones, fine-grained sandstones and volcanic tuffs. The layers of fine volcanic ash allowed accurate dating by the potassium /argon method. Lucy and other australopithecine specimens recovered display a variety of different primitive cranial post features, which indicate A. afarensis is distinct from other species of Australopithecus: small cranial capacity, palate similar to African apes (parallel tooth rows, shallow, long from front to back, narrow from side to side), primitive occipital, basal cranium anatomy, high frequency of unicuspid third premolars, prognathic face, and primitive mandibular anatomy. Postcranially, the pelvis, knee, ankle, and foot indicate habitual, terrestrial bipedalism, but ape-like curved finger and foot bones are retained ancestral ape-like features.

Question: Is it possible to determine the age of a fossil based on its location in the rock layer where it was found? If so, what are some methods for doing this?
Answer: Yes, one of the most famous fossils of all time - “Lucy” - found in Ethiopia by Donald Johanson in 1974 - was dated from adjacent rock layers. The fossil was found within the Hadar Formation, which consists of layers of mudstones, siltstones and fine-grained sandstones, interleaved with layers of tuff from local volcanoes. The fossil was dated by analyzing mineral crystals within the tuff. The first attempts at dating used the potassium/argon method. This method relies on the fact that Potassium 40 is unstable and decays with a half-life of 1.2 billion years. Most of the time the potassium decays to calcium but 11 percent of the time it decays to the gas argon. Within the molten lava, the argon can escape, but once a crystal forms, the argon is trapped. By measuring the amount of argon and potassium 40 in the crystal it is possible to determine when the crystal solidified. With Lucy, the efforts to determine age were hindered by several factors: the rocks in the recovery area were chemically altered or reworked by volcanic activity and datable crystals were very scarce in the sample material. The Lucy skeleton occurs in the part of the Hadar sequence that accumulated with the fastest rate of deposition, which partly accounts for her excellent preservation. In 1990 more samples were recovered and analyzed by the more accurate argon/argon method. The argon/argon method relies on the same potassium 40 to argon decay as the potassium/argon method but uses analysis of the different argon isotopes to determine the potassium content and can correct for contamination by atmospheric argon. In this method the mineral crystals are subjected to neutron irradiation in a nuclear reactor. The neutrons convert potassium 39 to argon 39. A standard sample of known age is subjected to the same irradiation. The samples are degassed by heating in a high vacuum. The gases are then analyzed by a mass spectrometer for argon 36, 39 and 40. The argon 36, which is in the atmosphere but is not produced by radioactive decay is used to estimate contamination. The adjusted argon 40 to argon 39 ratio is used to estimate the age by comparison with standard sample. The 1990 samples came from tuff layers 18 meters and 1 meter below the fossil strata. The ages came back 3.22 and 3.18 million years respectively. Dating the Lucy fossil was important in tracking the evolution of our ancestors.

Question: Why does liquid water exist on Earth but not on Titan, despite having a similar atmosphere?
Answer: The biggest difference between Earth and Titan is that Titan orbits the Sun at a distance almost ten times greater than the Earth’s orbit. This means that the intensity of the Sun’s heat and light is only 1% of the intensity at Earth. One consequence of Titans greater distance from the sun is that it was beyond the ice line and the soot line when it formed, and its composition is very different from Earth’s. Earth’s density is 5.5 tons per cubic meter. Titan’s density is 1.9 tons per cubic meter. Both bodies have rocky silicate material which has a density of 2.9 tons per cubic meter. Earth’s greater density is because it has an iron core. Titan’s lesser density is because it has a lot of water in its crust and mantle. Another consequence of Titan’s greater distance from the Sun is that its surface temperature is only minus 180 degrees Celsius, far below the freezing point of water. Titan’s surface and crust consists largely of frozen water ice. However, like Earth, Titan has a warmer interior, and it is believed liquid oceans of water exist below the surface. As a consequence of being beyond the soot line, Titan has a considerable amount of hydrocarbons, and has liquid hydrocarbon lakes on the surface, consisting mainly of liquid methane and ethane. Like Earth’s, Titan’s atmosphere consists mostly of nitrogen, but Titan has no oxygen, and the second most common gas is methane. Earth 78% nitrogen 21% oxygen, Titan 95% nitrogen, 5% methane. Despite Titan having an overall mass only 2% of Earth’s, Titans atmosphere is somewhat more massive than Earth’s. Radiation from the sun turns the hydrocarbons in Titan’s atmosphere into smog - making Titan’s atmosphere similar to Los Angeles.

Question: Which planets are considered inner planets? Why?
Answer: This is a little controversial and different astronomers count four, five or even six inner planets. The status of Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars as inner planets is recognized by everyone. These are planets relatively close to the sun and also share the characteristic of being rocky dense bodies distinct from the four outer gas giants Jupiter, Saturn. Uranus and Neptune. Then there is Ceres whose status has changed over the years since it was discovered in 1801 in an orbit between Mars and Jupiter. It was originally classified as a planet as it seemed a remarkable confirmation of the mathematical prediction of astronomer Johann Bode. In the 1860’s with many more objects discovered in this gap, most, but not all, astronomers reclassified it as an asteroid. Then in 2006 the International Astronomical Union (IAU) voted to accept a definition of a planet as a solar system object, in orbit around the sun, not a moon and of sufficient size to reach hydrostatic equilibrium. Then they added a further criterion, that a planet must have “cleared its neighborhood”, otherwise it is a dwarf planet. There are two things wrong with this definition. Firstly, they are classifying something as “dwarf” without reference to its size, whereas dwarf is commonly recognized to mean small. Secondly, they are excluding dwarf planets from planets - which goes against astronomical as well as common usage. A dwarf star is still a star. A dwarf galaxy is still a galaxy. And under the original etymology a dwarf is still a human. Ceres also matches the characteristics of the other inner planets. It has reached hydrostatic equilibrium (roughly round shape), it is largely composed of rocky material, it has a (thin) atmosphere and a differentiated structure with a crust and a mantle, and possibly a core. As for the sixth “planet”, there is a paper by professional astronomers, which argues that moons are planets, based mainly on their composition. If so, the only moon to qualify as an inner planet would be our Moon since the moons of Mars are too small to have reached hydrostatic equilibrium. Thus, we could reach six inner planets Mercury, Venus, Moon, Earth, Mars and Ceres.

Question: Is coal imported into England?
Answer: I studied mining engineering at Newcastle University in England in the 1960s. I remember visiting one mine producing 1.5 million tons per year with a workforce of 2,200 men. And they were all men. In the 1990s I was Vice President of the Southern Region of BHP Coal in Queensland Australia. I was responsible for five mines - four surface mines and one underground longwall mine. The most productive was the longwall mine. It put out 5.6 million tons per year with 220 employees - including some women. I remember at the official mine opening, Jerry Ellis, the CEO of BHP was chatting to some employees. Among them was a female underground diesel fitter. He asked her if she had ever experienced harassment. Another (male) employee standing nearby said, with a grin on his face, “we wouldn’t dare”. As an example of the potential of the longwall method, our coalface could and frequently did put out 3,000 tons per hour. With 8,760 hours in a year, theoretically we could reach 25 million tons. The actual output of 5.6 million, while commendable, means that we were only achieving 22% of possible production. The near 80% idle time was due to equipment breakdowns, shift changes, roof problems, infrastructure problems, longwall panel moves and similar issues. Favourable geological conditions are one reason for more productive coal mining in Australia and the US, but the British industry certainly did things that contributed to its downfall. The reluctance to implement newer methods was one handicap - for example it took a long time for roofbolting to become a standard support method. I would like to think that enlightened management was another reason for higher productivity in Australia. Coal from BHP coal was and is exported to many countries including Japan, China, Brazil and European countries, including the UK. High productivity in Australia combined with large volume low-cost shipping means that Australian coal is competitive in price even after being shipped 12,000 miles. While I was at Newcastle, there was great excitement at the promise of the new Selby complex - then in very early planning. But Selby never lived up to its promise.

Question: Does the amount of helium in the atmosphere support a young Earth?
Answer: The claim that the helium content of the atmosphere is evidence of a young Earth is made by the Institute of Creation Research at The Age of the Earth's Atmosphere Estimated by its Helium Content | The Institute for Creation Research. The low concentration of helium actually measured would suggest that the earth’s atmosphere must be quite young.” They quote a paper presented by Larry Vardiman, PhD at the First Creation Conference in 1986. Question: How are oxygen isotope records of marine sediments used to understand glacial-interglacial cycles?
Answer: Oxygen has three stable isotopes. Oxygen 16, whose nucleus contains 8 protons, and 8 neutrons makes up 99.76% of the oxygen in the atmosphere. Oxygen 17, with 8 protons, and nine neutrons makes up 0.04%, and oxygen 18 with 8 protons and 10 neutrons makes up 0.2%. Oxygen isotope analysis usually measures the ratio of oxygen 18 to oxygen 16. Because water containing Oxygen 18 is 11% heavier than water with Oxygen 16 and because the extra neutrons affect the hydrogen bonds, water with Oxygen 18 requires more energy to vaporize and releases more energy when it condenses and diffuses less readily than water with Oxygen 16. Note that heavy water with two atoms of deuterium has similar properties to water with Oxygen 18, but deuterium makes up only 0.01% of hydrogen and water with two atoms of deuterium is very rare. In the global circulation water tends to be evaporated from the oceans in the warmer lower latitudes and precipitates out as rain as winds move it towards the poles. Because the water containing Oxygen 18 is harder to evaporate and easier to precipitate, precipitation at higher latitudes is depleted in Oxygen 18. During glacial periods this depleted water may be locked up in glacial ice and does not return to the ocean. In consequence the water in the oceans becomes enriched in Oxygen 18. Carbon dioxide dissolved in the water reacts with water molecules to form carbonic acid (H2CO3), which ionizes to two hydrogen ions and a carbonate ion (CO3 - -). If the water molecule contains Oxygen 18, the carbonate ion will contain two atoms of Oxygen 16 and one atom of Oxygen 18. Shelly creatures react calcium ions in the water with the carbonate ions to form calcium carbonate (CaCO3), which they use to build their shells. Shells which are formed during glacial periods will thus be very slightly enriched with Oxygen 18, compared to Oxygen 16. The shells of choice used for analysis are the abundant tiny foraminifera. The ratio of Oxygen 18 to Oxygen 16 can be accurately determined with a mass spectrometer. The above is a simplified explanation. The paper at gives a much more thorough explanation. The chart below (and the image of foraminifera above) are taken from this paper. Because natural fractionations are, in practice, quite small, and Oxygen 18 is always very much rarer than Oxygen 16, the isotopic ratios of natural materials are generally quite close to the average value. Small differences between small numbers are un-wieldy, so (as is the convention for other stable isotope systems) oxygen isotope ratios are generally quoted as deviations (delta values) from the oxygen isotope ratio (δ18O) of a standard sub-stance in parts per thousand ('per mil', signified by the symbol, ‘‰’). There are good, practical reasons for this convention because isotope ratios of sample materials are almost always measured relative to a laboratory standard rather than as an absolute ratio, which is much more difficult to determine accurately. Note that if a sample has a positive δ18O, it is said to be enriched in the heavy isotope relative to the standard and, if negative, it is said to be depleted. It so happens that two different standard values are in widespread use from which these delta-values are quoted: Vienna Standard Mean Ocean Water (VSMOW) and Vienna Pee Dee Belemnite (VPDB, which is a carbonate standard.

Question: The atomic clock on the moon is 58.7 microseconds faster than the atomic clock on Earth. Is time itself fast or slow? Or is the clock unstable?
Answer: As yet there are no atomic clocks on the moon, but as described at NASA Will Create a New Time Zone for the Moon, Called Coordinated Lunar Time future atomic clocks on the moon will indeed run faster than atomic clocks on Earth by 58.7 microseconds per day. This is a small difference, and it will take 46 years for the difference to accumulate to one whole second. The reason for the difference in speed is due to the combination of two opposing relativity effects. As predicted in Einstein’s Theory of Special Relativity, clocks which are moving tick slower than those that are at rest. Since the moon is rotating around the Earth, this effect causes the clocks to tick slower on the moon. In contrast, Einstein’s Theory of General Relativity predicts that clocks in lower gravity fields will tick faster. Thus, because the moon is less massive and has a weaker gravity field than the Earth the clocks on the moon click faster. The gravity effect is stronger than the velocity effect and so the net effect is that the moon clocks tick faster. GPS satellites orbiting Earth are also affected by relativity. Their clocks gain 38.6 microseconds per day relative to those on the surface of the Earth. The need for precise timing for navigation is one reason why NASA is seeking international agreement on a standard for lunar time - as described at The Moon May Soon Have Its Own Time Zone . The Wikipedia site below explains the time effects on GPS satellites The graph from Wikipedia does not extend as far as the moon, but it gives a good graphic of the opposing effects.

Question: How long does it take for the Earth to replenish its oxygen supply?
Answer: The oxygen cycle is complementary to the carbon cycle. According to Carbon cycle - Wikipedia land plants absorb 121 billion metric tons of carbon every year in the form of carbon dioxide. In doing so they release 323 billion metric tons of oxygen (121 x 32/ 12). In scientific notation this is 3.23 x 10^11 metric tons The oceans of the world are more or less in balance on carbon dioxide and do not release significant quantities of oxygen. The mass of the Earth’s atmosphere is 5.15 x 10^15 metric tons. Oxygen makes up 20.95% of the atmosphere by volume and 23.1 % by mass. The mass of oxygen in the atmosphere is thus 1.19 x 10^15 metric tons. Dividing 1.19 x 10^15 by 3.23 x 10^11 gives us 3,690 years. This is the time plants take to replace all the atmospheric oxygen.

Question: What led to the change in the definition of a planet? What were the issues with the previous definition?
Answer: It’s worth recalling the actual resolution from the 2006 International Astronomical Union (IAU) meeting: RESOLUTION 5A The IAU therefore resolves that "planets" and other bodies in our Solar System be defined into three distinct categories in the following way: (1) A "planet" (see note 1) is a celestial body that (a) is in orbit around the Sun, (b) has sufficient mass for its self-gravity to overcome rigid body forces so that it assumes a hydrostatic equilibrium (nearly round) shape, and (c) has cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit. (2) A "dwarf planet" is a celestial body that (a) is in orbit around the Sun, (b) has sufficient mass for its self-gravity to overcome rigid body forces so that it assumes a hydrostatic equilibrium (nearly round) shape (see note 2) , (c) has not cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit, and (d) is not a satellite. (3) All other objects (see note 3) except satellites orbiting the Sun shall be referred to collectively as "Small Solar-System Bodies". Note 1 The eight planets are: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Note 2 An IAU process will be established to assign borderline objects into either dwarf planet and other categories. Note 3 These currently include most of the Solar System asteroids, most Trans-Neptunian Objects (TNOs), comets, and other small bodies. The above is the actual resolution that was approved at the end of the meeting when many delegates had left, except that I have had to adjust for the fact that Quora does not allow superscripts. Astronomy developed for many years with everyone understanding the meaning of common terms like galaxy, solar system, star, planet, satellite, comet and asteroid. The problem of definitions has arisen because of the discovery of objects which lie intermediate to these categories. The specific issue in this case was the discovery of trans neptunium objects comparable to Pluto. Other borderline questions are: is a globular cluster not attached to a galaxy, a “galaxy”; is a brown dwarf a “star”; is a temporary natural object in orbit around the Earth, like 2020 CD3 a “moon”; is a light object like ‘Oumuamua a “comet” or an “asteroid”. In my opinion there are a number of problems with the IAU definitions: It is interesting to note that just before the 2006 meeting, the IAU issued a press release in which they said Pluto was a planet. In fact, not only was Pluto a planet, but also Charon (a moon or co-planet of Pluto), Ceres, and another trans Neptunium body were also planets - making 12 planets in all in the Solar System. The text of the press release reads in part “If the definition is approved by the astronomers gathered 14-25 August 2006 at the IAU General Assembly in Prague, our Solar System will include 12 planets, with more to come: eight classical planets that dominate the system, three planets in a new and growing category of "plutons" - Pluto-like objects - and Ceres. Pluto remains a planet and is the prototype for the new category of "plutons."” Exactly why the meeting decided to disregard the special committee they had appointed to review the issue and instead came up with cockeyed alternative is a mystery. Question: How much total distance has been tracked by GPS of movement from the Pacific Plate? Asked AI, said it doesn’t have access to this data. Does that mean it has never been published? If so why not? Is tectonics even science?
Answer: The Pacific plate is the largest plate on Earth. Paul Tregonning (Australian National University), Michael Bevis (Ohio State University) and Tenuyuki Kato (University of Tokyo) published a joint paper in the October 2002 edition of The Journal of Geophysical Research called Motion and Rigidity of the Pacific Plate and Implications for Plate Boundary Deformation. It is available at To understand the paper, you have to understand spherical geometry - which I have to admit I found to be a very difficult part of our surveying course in my university mining engineering degree. A rigid plate moving over a sphere will not have the same velocity everywhere. In particular, you need to understand Euler's rotation theorem, which states that, in three-dimensional space, any displacement of a rigid body such that a point on the rigid body remains fixed, is equivalent to a single rotation about some axis that runs through the fixed point. In the case of a sphere, like the Earth, the fixed point is the centre of the sphere. Thus the asis of rotation is necessarily a diameter of the sphere. The theorem is named after Leonhard Euler, who proved it in 1775. The axis of rotation is known as a Euler axis, typically represented by a unit vector ê. Its product by the rotation angle is known as an axis-angle vector. The conclusion of Tregonning et al’s paper is that the Pacific plate is rotating around an axis that runs through 63.75 S, 110.86 E at 0.677 degrees per million years. The paper notes the following velocities of GPS stations. Vn is the velocity north in mm per year, Ve is the velocity east. Since the plate is moving westwards, the latter movement is shown negative. Thus, Auckland Island, in the South Pacific is moving at 28.1 mm per year to the north and 29.2 mm per year to the west (45.5 mm/year net), whereas Marcus Island in the North Pacific is moving at 21.8 mm per year to the north and 72.3 mm per year to the west (75.5 mm/year net). And of course, Plate Tectonics is a science. As a mining engineer, my idea of a valuable science is one that finds exploitable mineral resources. The ideas of plate tectonics have led to many discoveries. But I am not sure that AI is a science. Microsoft claims that Bing uses AI, but as you found it fails to find relevant papers. Question: Is Noah's flood scientifically plausible?
Answer: A worldwide flood is a possibility in the remote future. The oceans of the world are estimated to contain 1.335 billion cubic kilometers of water. The surface area of the Earth is 500 million square kilometers. Dividing one by the other shows that if the Earth was smooth, it would be covered with an ocean with an average depth of 2,617 meters (8,588 feet). The Earth is currently divided into two separate regimes - land and water. The average depth of the oceans is 3865 meters below sea level, whereas the average height of the land is 841 meters above sea level. There are powerful forces working to even out the extremes. Erosion, especially running water, attacks the high areas while sedimentation fills in the oceans. Waves and storms attack the coast, breaking down even high cliffs. Acid rain dissolves limestone, carrying its substance into the oceans. It is true that on the scale of human lifetimes erosion is slow, but on the geological scale of millions of years it would be sufficient to even out the surface. This would have happened long ago, were it not for the even more powerful force of plate tectonics. Colliding plates build mountain ranges, either through the agency of volcanoes or by simple uplift. The Earth’s highest mountain range, the Himalayas, is still climbing despite the best efforts of erosion. The energy that drives plate tectonics is left-over heat from the Earth’s formation, heat from the decay of radioactive elements and latent heat from the slowly solidifying liquid core. The heat of formation is leaking away, the radioactive elements are decaying and getting less energetic every year, and the core will eventually all be solid. Thus, the building force of plate tectonics gets less over time, whereas the erosive forces remain unchanged. Eventually the erosive forces will be more powerful than the building forces and the Earth will slowly change to a smooth form with a worldwide ocean. As for the mechanics of the ark itself, John Woodmarappe has written a very detailed book called “Noah’s Ark - a Feasibility Study”, which attempts to prove that it was possible for the ark to contain 16,000 animals, and it was possible for Noah and his seven-person crew to feed and care for them. The book iss available on Amazon for $A91. Glenn Morton has written a critical review pointing issues and discrepancies at and Woodmarappe has fired back with refutation of the points raised by Morton at John Woodmorappe’s refutation of Glen Morton’s review of NOAH’S ARK: A FEASIBILITY STUDY I side with Morton, but the interchange is entertaining.

Question: If all of the world’s oceans were to flood every piece of land on earth, how deep would the water be on average?
Answer: The Earth’s oceans contain 1.335 billion cubic kilometers of water. The surface area of the Earth is 500 million square kilometers. Dividing one by the other shows that if the Earth did not have anomalous highs and lows, it would be covered with an ocean with an average depth of 2,617 meters (8,588 feet). The Earth is currently divided into two separate regimes - land and water. The average depth of the oceans is 3865 meters, whereas the average height of the land is 841 meters. There are small areas of extremes, with mountains as high as 8,848 meters above sea level and ocean trenches as low as 11,033 meters below sea level. There are powerful forces working to even out the extremes. Erosion, especially running water, attacks the high areas while sedimentation fills in the oceans. Opposing these forces is the even more powerful force of plate tectonics, driven by convection plumes in the mantle. Where oceanic plates collide, one is forced under the other, creating a deep trench. The famous Marianas Trench has been created by the Pacific Plate diving under the Philippine Sea Plate. Where continental plates collide huge mountain ranges are created. The Himalayas are still rising where the Indian Plate collides with the Eurasian plate. The energy driving the mantle convection plumes derives from the radioactive decay of uranium, thorium and potassium. The heat from radioactive decay slowly subsides as the elements are used up. One day in the future, the heat will no longer be sufficient to drive the convection currents. Then the forces of erosion and sedimentation will be triumphant. The mountains will erode down and the trenches fill with sediment. The surface of the Earth will approach a uniform elevation. Then we could have a water world - a planet completely covered in water to a depth of 2,617 meters. But there is another factor to take into account. As the sun ages its core will expand, increasing the zone of nuclear fusion and increasing the heat output of the sun. The sun already emits considerably more energy than when it first formed, and this trend will continue. This could be sufficient to drive off Earth’s water. So, the future of Earth - water world or desert world - depends on the balance between the declining heat from radioactive decay in the Earth’s mantle and the increasing heat from an aging sun. Either way, it’s a few billion years in the future. So, I would recommend waiting a while before you start building an ark, or investing in camels.

Question: Why is natural uranium not readily available on the earth's surface? Why is it necessary to extract it before using it as fuel in reactors?
Answer: Metallic uranium is very reactive and can ignite spontaneously when exposed to air. As a result, uranium is never found as a native metal, but always as a compound - often an oxide. But uranium compounds are common in rocks. Granite averages 35 parts per million of uranium but can vary from 10 to 100 parts per million. A typical fuel pellet used in a power reactor consists of uranium dioxide, which 88% (880,000 parts per million) uranium. Moreover, fuel pellets typically consist of 3 to 5% Uranium 235, whereas ore in the ground is only 0.7% U235. The enrichment process is only 55 to 65% efficient. Typically, it takes 8 kilograms of uranium dioxide to make 1 kilogram of uranium dioxide fuel. Using current technology, the 1 Kilogram fuel pellet can generate as much power as 16 tons of coal. If the uranium in the fuel pellet was originally from a typical granite, it would take 228 tons of granite to make a 1-kilogram fuel pellet. Fortunately, most uranium mines have access to higher grade ore. A low-grade ore would be about 1,000 parts per million - requiring only 8 tons of ore to end up with a 1 kg fuel pellet. The world's richest uranium mine, Cigar Lake in Canada, has ore which runs 17% (170,000 parts per million) of uranium. A 1 Kg fuel pellet can be sourced from just 47 Kilograms of Cigar Lake ore.

Question: Is a global flood possible on Earth? If so, how long would it take for all oceans to cover all land? What is the maximum amount of water that could fit inside Earth's volume?
Answer: A global flood seems entirely possible. The Earth’s oceans contain 1.335 billion cubic kilometers of water. The surface area of the Earth is 500 million square kilometers. Dividing one by the other shows that if the Earth did not have anomalous highs and lows, it would be covered with an ocean with an average depth of 2,617 meters (8,588 feet). The Earth is currently divided into two separate regimes - land and water. The average depth of the oceans is 3865 meters, whereas the average height of the land is 841 meters. There are small areas of extremes, with mountains as high as 8,848 meters above sea level and ocean trenches as low as 11,033 meters below sea level. There are powerful forces working to even out the extremes. Erosion, especially running water, attacks the high areas while sedimentation fills in the oceans. Opposing these forces is the even more powerful force of plate tectonics, driven by convection plumes in the mantle. Where oceanic plates collide, one is forced under the other, creating a deep trench. The famous Marianas Trench has been created by the Pacific Plate diving under the Philippine Sea Plate. Where continental plates collide huge mountain ranges are created. The Himalayas are still rising where the Indian Plate collides with the Eurasian plate. The energy driving the mantle convection plumes derives from the radioactive decay of uranium, thorium and potassium. The heat from radioactive decay slowly subsides as the elements are used up. One day in the future, the heat will no longer be sufficient to drive the convection currents. Then the forces of erosion and sedimentation will be triumphant. The mountains will erode down and the trenches fill with sediment. The surface of the Earth will approach a uniform elevation. This could result in a global flood. But another development could preclude this outcome. As the sun ages its core will expand, increasing the zone of nuclear fusion and increasing the heat output of the sun. This could be sufficient to drive off Earth’s water. So, the future of Earth depends on the balance between the declining heat from radioactive decay in the Earth’s mantle and the increasing heat from an aging sun. Either way, it’s a few billion years in the future. So, I would recommend waiting a while before you start building an ark, or investing in camels.

Question: What are the gases present in Earth's atmosphere and why are they there? What are their properties, effects, and potential uses?
Answer: In seeking clues to the origin of gasses in the Earth’s atmosphere it is instructive to compare the composition of Earth’s atmosphere with that of sister planet Venus. The most striking difference is the fact that carbon dioxide is the dominant gas on Venus but is a minor constituent of Earth’s atmosphere. It is likely that the atmosphere of the newly formed Earth was similar to that of Venus. Life, and especially the blue-green algae in the oceans, has converted Earth’s original carbon dioxide to carbon solids (like coal) or liquids (like oil), and oxygen. Some of the oxygen has remained in the atmosphere, but a larger fraction has combined with other elements especially iron. The huge iron deposits of Australia and Brazil are the result of oxidation of dissolved iron in the Earth’s oceans. Nitrogen is the dominant gas in Earth’s atmosphere, but only the second most common gas in the atmosphere of Venus. The removal of the carbon dioxide from Earth’s atmosphere has resulted in the dominance of nitrogen. Nitrogen is a generally non-reactive gas, which is why it survives in Earth’s atmosphere. In intense condition, such as inside lightning strikes, nitrogen will react with oxygen, forming soluble nitrates. These are essential for life. The principal use of nitrogen is in the manufacture of fertilizers and explosives, usually starting with Haber process where nitrogen is combined with hydrogen to make ammonia. Oxygen is the second most common gas in the Earth’s atmosphere, but only exists in tiny amounts as atomic oxygen in the atmosphere of Venus. As noted above it exists in Earth’s atmosphere (mostly in diatomic molecular form) as a result of the reduction of carbon dioxide by plants. Very small amounts are present in atomic form and in the triatomic molecule ozone, which is important for protecting us from the sun’s ultraviolet radiation. It is a highly reactive element. The most important use for humans is in breathing, without which our lives are not possible. Another important use is fire and combustion of all kinds. Argon is the third most abundant gas in Earth’s atmosphere. The fact that the most abundant of the three stable argon isotopes is Argon 40 suggests that most of the Earth’s argon originated from the radioactive decay of Potassium 40. Venus has almost the same amount of argon as Earth in its atmosphere, but the concentration is diluted down by the thick carbon dioxide atmosphere. Argon is one of the very unreactive noble gasses. It is used as an inert atmosphere for specialized welding and other applications. Water Vapor - is the fourth most abundant gas in the atmosphere. The concentration is very variable, which is why atmospheric compositions of other gasses are usually quoted on a dry basis. While overall the water vapor content of our atmosphere is 0.4%, at sea level the average composition is more like 1%. Due to its rapid rotation and liquid iron core, Earth has a significant magnetic field, which deflects the sun’s solar wind. Venus has a very slow rotation rate (243 Earth days) and no significant magnetic field. Venus also has high surface temperatures (482 degrees C). The combination has resulted in most of the water of Venus being blown away by the solar wind. Water on Earth is protected by the magnetic field. Some may be from the original proto- Earth and some may have been added by collisions with comets. Our bodies and all life on Earth are based on chemical reactions in which water is involved. And of course, water has many uses too innumerable to list here. Carbon Dioxide is the fifth most abundant gas in our atmosphere, and as discussed above was a much bigger component of the atmosphere of the early Earth. Carbon dioxide is essential for plant growth and without it, food production would cease. Carbon dioxide cycles quite rapidly through the atmosphere and plants. The atmosphere currently contains about 3.4 trillion tons of carbon dioxide. Plants absorb about 0.63 trillion tons every year. Hence the carbon dioxide completely cycles in just 5.4 years. Human use of fossil fuels has increased the carbon dioxide content of the atmosphere by 50% (from 280 to 420 ppm) in the last 200 years. Currently fossil fuel use adds about 1.1% to the carbon dioxide in the Earth’s atmosphere every year. The removal of the carbon dioxide partly explains why Earth’s atmosphere is only a little more than 1% of the density of the atmosphere of Venus. Neon - the sixth most abundant gas in our atmosphere and like argon, neon is an unreactive noble gas. It is more abundant than argon in the universe but unlike argon is not the product of radioactive decay of a common element. It is used in signs. Helium - the seventh most abundant gas in the Earth’s atmosphere. The helium atom is light enough that some can reach escape velocity in the upper atmosphere and leave the Earth. Almost all of Earth’s original supply of helium has escaped in this fashion. It has been supplemented by the radioactive decay of uranium and thorium minerals. Helium has two stable isotopes, Helium 3 and Helium 4. In interstellar space there is about one atom of Helium 3 for every 10,000 atoms of Helium 4, but on Earth the ratio is one atom of Helium 3 for every million atoms of Helium 4. This is because only Helium 4 is released by radioactive decay. Helium is extracted from natural gas to fill children’s balloons and large-scale blimps. Methane - methane is the main component in natural gas. Most methane in the atmosphere is likely the result of escape from natural gas reservoirs. It is also produced from decaying vegetation. Human extraction of natural gas has doubled the concentration in the atmosphere. Methane is a widely used fossil fuel. Extraction from the atmosphere is possible but uneconomic compared to natural gas. Krypton - like argon and neon is another noble gas. Like neon, it is used in signs. Sulfur Dioxide - is negligible in the Earth’s atmosphere as a whole but can be present near sources of pollution, like coal fired power plants. It is soluble in water and is quickly washed out of the Earth’s atmosphere - as “acid rain”. Venus is much dryer and the sulfur dioxide there combines with some of the water to make sulfuric acid clouds.

Question: What keeps Earth's inner molten core hot enough to maintain a global magnetic field instead of cooling down like a lava lamp?
Answer: In 1862, the physicist William Thompson (later Lord Kelvin) calculated the age of the Earth based on the time taken to cool from a molten state. His answer was between 20 million and 400 million years. Thompson did not know about and did not include in his calculation three factors that have slowed the cooling of the Earth, whose age is now estimated at about 4.3 billion years, 10 times longer than Thompson’s upper estimate. The three factors are: Radioactive decay. The early Earth contained many unstable atoms. Their decay added to the heat of the early Earth. Most of these unstable atoms had relatively short half-lives - for example aluminum 26 has a half-life less than a million years. These atoms have all decayed and no longer contribute to the heat of the Earth. However, four longer lived isotopes are still active and still provide heat. These are: potassium 40 (half-life 1.2 billion years); uranium 235 (half-life 0.7 billion years); uranium 238 (half-life 4.5 billion years) and thorium 232 (half-life 14.1 billion years). These four isotopes are mostly in the mantle of the Earth where they reduce heat flow from the core. As these isotopes decay, the heat they produce is slowly reducing. Latent heat. The inner core of the Earth is solid - probably a crystalline form of iron. The solidification of liquid iron from the outer core is providing latent heat. As the solid core increases in size, the contribution from this source is likely increasing. Tidal friction. The Moon’s gravity as it rotates around the Earth produces friction between the layers of the Earth, resulting in heating. This source of heat has greatly reduced as a result of the Moon getting further from the Earth.

Answer: The Earth’s core contains about one-third the mass of the planet, and it is at a temperature of at least 5,000 degrees Celsius. Assuming the mass of the core is 1.9 x 10^24 Kg and the specific heat of the core material is 500 Joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, the energy in the core works out to 4.8 x 10^30 Joules. The current consumption of fossil fuels is about 15 billion tons of coal equivalent per year. The average heat content is around 30 Megajoules per Kg. The energy in a year’s consumption of fossil fuels is therefore 15 x 10^9 x 10^3 x 30 x10^6 = 4.5 x 10^20 Joules. Assuming that there is enough fossil fuel to last another 200 years at this rate, then the total energy of Earth’s fossil fuels is 9 x 10^22. Dividing 4.8 x 10^30 by 9 x 10^22 gives a figure of 53 million. That is, there is 53 million times more energy in the core than in all the reserves of Earth’s fossil fuels. Getting that energy however is difficult. The core lies some 2,900 kilometers below the surface. The deepest hole ever drilled only penetrated a pathetic 12 kilometers down. Going deeper presents immense problems. One of the very problems is the heat of the material being penetrated. Steel loses its strength at high temperatures. Drilling mud, essential for lubricating the cutting head and transporting cuttings to the surface, will boil and become useless. Of course, some of the energy of the core is continually leaking upwards. However, the amount of power generated is far short of that generated from fossil fuels. One of the problems with geothermal energy comes back to the temperature problems involved in drilling. The theoretical maximum efficiency of a steam turbine is determined by the difference between the heat source and the heat sink. With a heat source only a little above the 100 degree boiling point of water, the theoretical efficiency is less than 25% and the actual efficiency is even less. Fossil fuel plants can heat water to 600 degrees C, giving far higher efficiency.

Question: How many elements beyond uranium have been discovered and where can they be found on Earth?
Answer: As of January 2024, there are 26 known and discovered elements heavier than uranium. While a few like plutonium are widely dispersed through the environment due to bomb testing, and some like americium have applications in consumer devices, the heavier ones can only be made in laboratories. The really heavy ones are only made a few atoms at a time, and then they quickly decay. The elements up to 100 - Fermium can be made by neutron capture. Because fermium isotopes are unstable, elements after fermium must be made by fusing lighter elements. The 26 are: Element 93 Neptunium – Neptunium is present in nuclear waste. It is also generated in reactors as part of the process to synthesize plutonium. Neptunium is found in old ionization-chamber smoke detectors, which used Americium 241. Neptunium is on the decay chain of Americium. The detectors start with 0.2 micrograms of americium. After 20 years, 0.006 micrograms (3%) will have decayed to neptunium. Element 94 Plutonium. The human body contains small amounts of plutonium as a result of nuclear bomb testing. Plutonium is in nuclear weapons. Plutonium is used as a fuel in some nuclear power plants – especially in Europe. Element 95 Americium. Americium is widespread in small quantities as a result of nuclear bomb testing. Trinitite, the glassy residue left on the desert floor near Alamogordo, New Mexico, after the plutonium-based Trinity nuclear bomb test on 16 July 1945, contains traces of americium-241. Americium is widely used in smoke detectors and has other uses. Element 96 Curium. Curium is present in nuclear waste. It has been used as an alpha particle source – for example in alpha particle X-ray spectrometers (APXS). These instruments have been sent into space and were installed on the Sojourner, Mars, Mars 96, Mars Exploration Rovers and Philae comet lander. Element 97 Berkelium. Berkelium is present in small quantities in nuclear waste and bomb residues. Element 98 Californium. Californium is found in nuclear waste and bomb residues. It is used as a neutron source – for example in instant ash analyzers in the coal industry. It is very radioactive. Element 99 Einsteinium. Einsteinium isotopes are short lived – the longest has a half life of 471 days. It is produced in hydrogen bombs and in specialist high energy nuclear reactors. It is used as a starting material for heavier elements and thus can be found in research laboratories. Element 100 Fermium. Fermium is produced in small quantities in hydrogen bomb explosions. It can be created in the lab by bombarding plutonium with neutrons. It has no applications. The longest living isotope has a half-life of 100 days. Element 101 Mendelevium. Mendelevium can be made in the laboratory by bombarding Einsteinium with alpha particles. It does not occur naturally or in nuclear waste or bomb residues. The longest-lived isotope has a half-life of 51 days Element 102 Nobelium. Nobelium is made in the laboratory by bombarding californium of einsteinium with oxygen ions. It does not occur naturally or in nuclear waste or bomb residues. The longest-lived isotope has a half-life of 58 minutes. Element 103 Lawrencium. Lawrencium is made in the laboratory by bombarding californium or einsteinium with boron ions. It does not occur naturally or in nuclear waste or bomb residues. The longest-lived isotope has a half-life of 11 hours. Element 104 Rutherfordium. Rutherfordium is made in the laboratory by bombarding californium with carbon ions. It does not occur naturally or in nuclear waste or bomb residues. The longest-lived isotope has a half-life of 15 minutes. Element 105 Dubnium. Dubnium is made in the laboratory by bombarding californium with neon ions. It does not occur naturally or in nuclear waste or bomb residues. The longest-lived isotope has a half-life of 16 hours. Element 106 Seaborgium. Seaborgium is made in the laboratory by bombarding californium with oxygen 18 ions. It does not occur naturally or in nuclear waste or bomb residues. The longest-lived isotope has a half-life of 14 minutes. Element 107 Bohrium. Bohrium is made in the laboratory by bombarding bismuth with chromium 54 ions. It does not occur naturally or in nuclear waste or bomb residues. The longest-lived isotope has a half-life of 11.5 minutes. Element 108 Hassium. Hassium is made in the laboratory by bombarding lead with iron ions. It does not occur naturally or in nuclear waste or bomb residues. The longest-lived isotope has a half-life of 130 seconds. Element 109 Meitnerium. Meitnerium is made in the laboratory by bombarding bismuth with iron ions. It does not occur naturally or in nuclear waste or bomb residues. The longest-lived isotope has a half-life of 76 seconds. Element 110 Darmstadtium. Darmstadtium is made in the laboratory by bombarding lead with nickel ions. It does not occur naturally or in nuclear waste or bomb residues. The longest-lived isotope has a half-life of 14 seconds. Element 111 Roentgenium. Roentgenium is made in the laboratory by bombarding bismuth with nickel ions. It does not occur naturally or in nuclear waste or bomb residues. The longest-lived isotope has a half-life of 10 minutes. Element 112 Copernicium. Copernicium is made in the laboratory by bombarding zinc with lead ions. The initial discovery made only one atom of Copernicium. It does not occur naturally or in nuclear waste or bomb residues. The longest-lived isotope has a half-life of 8.4 seconds. Element 113 Nihonium. Nihonium is made in the laboratory by bombarding thallium with zinc ions. The longest-lived isotope has a half-life of 10 seconds. Element 114 Flerovium. Flerovium is made in the laboratory by bombarding plutonium with calcium ions. The longest-lived isotope has a half-life of 19 seconds. Element 115 Moscovium. Moscovium is made in the laboratory by bombarding americium with calcium ions. The longest-lived isotope has a half-life of 650 milliseconds. Element 116 Livermorium. Livermorium is made in the laboratory by bombarding curium with calcium ions. The longest-lived isotope has a half-life of 80 milliseconds. Element 117 Tennessine. Tennessine is made in the laboratory by bombarding berkelium with calcium ions. The longest-lived isotope has a half-life of 51 milliseconds. Element 118 Oganesson. Oganesson is made in the laboratory by bombarding californium with calcium ions. The longest-lived isotope has a half-life of 0.7 milliseconds. Element 119. No element 119 has yet been found. Question: How much energy does it take to boil water on Earth's surface?

In US units it will take about 9,300 British Thermal Units (BTU) to turn one gallon (8.34 pounds) of water at 68 degrees F into steam at 212 degrees F.. Coincidently 9,300 BTUs is about the energy content of the low-grade coal typically used in power plants. Thus, it takes the energy of a pound of coal to convert a gallon of water to steam.

Question: Why does carbon occur naturally on Earth, but silicon does not?
Answer: Silicon is much more common in the Earth than carbon. Silicon accounts for about 17%(170,000 parts per million) of the atoms in the Earth, whereas carbon is only about 300 parts per million (0.03%) of the Earth. This is in contrast to the solar system as a whole where carbon is five times more abundant than silicon. This disparity arose because carbon and silicon in the early solar system both combined with oxygen to make carbon dioxide and silica. The crucial difference is that carbon dioxide is much more volatile than silica and was expelled from the inner solar system. The reason elemental carbon exists on the Earth, and elemental silicon does not is entirely due to life. Plants split carbon dioxide into carbohydrates and oxygen. In favourable circumstances the carbohydrates produced by the plants are buried and heat and pressure convert the carbohydrates to elemental carbon and water. The elemental oxygen in the atmosphere and the elemental carbon in coal, carbonaceous shale and other rocks is entirely the cumulative effect of billions of years of plant life, and the coalification process. There is no corresponding process making elemental silicon.

Question: How does radioactive decay only occur in the mantle and crust? Why can’t it start decaying in the outer/inner core?
Answer: When the Earth formed from an accumulation of smaller bodies in the early solar system, the gravitational and collisional energy released caused the earth to melt. The material in the molten Earth segregated into an iron fraction and a rocky silicate fraction. Molten iron and molten silicates are like oil and water - they don’t mix. Certain elements preferred to segregate with the iron fraction - they are called siderophile (iron loving) elements. Other elements preferred to join the silicate fraction - they are known as lithophile (rock loving) elements. Siderophile elements include gold and platinum, which is why the core of the Earth is much richer in these precious metals than the crust. Importantly the elements uranium, thorium and potassium are lithophile - they went with the rocky mantle and crust, leaving little or none in the core. Initially there were many radioactive isotopes dispersed throughout the Earth. Iron 60 and Aluminium 26 were particularly plentiful. But most of these elements had only short half lives. Aluminium 26 has a half life of only 700,000 years and iron 60’s half life is only 2.7 million years. In the 4.3 billion years since the formation of the Earth, most of these elements have long since decayed to insignificantly low levels. The only significant remaining radioactive isotopes are those with relatively long half lives. Uranium 235 has a half life of 700 million years, uranium 238 is at 4.5 billion years, thorium 232 is at 14 billion years and potassium 40 is at 1.2 billion years. These four isotopes make up almost all the remaining radioactive materials in the Earth. All four are lithophile, which is why they are in the mantle and crust and not in the core.

Question: What is the reason that gold is not found as native metal in nature, but geologists believe that much of what exists today has formed at great depths within earth’s core under high pressure and heat conditions?

It weighed 109.6 kilograms (3,523 troy ounces) and today the gold content would be worth $3.5 million. Besides nuggets, much gold is tiny disseminated particles of pure gold. Many gold deposits are the result of hot fluids circulating through magma, dissolving the gold and then depositing it when chemical conditions change. There are some non native metal gold minerals such as the gold tellurides, but they are relatively rare. Gold was not formed in the core of the Earth but was formed in exploding stars during supernova eruptions by the r- (rapid neutron-capture) process. When the Earth consolidated from asteroids in the early solar system it differentiated into an iron core and a rocky mantle. Lithophile (“rock loving”) elements preferentially went to the mantle and siderophile (“iron-loving”) elements ended up in the core. Gold is a siderophile element and most gold ended up in the core. The process was not 100% perfect and some gold (and some iron) ended up in the mantle. The crust later differentiated from the mantle. The gold we find in the crust now is either the tiny remnants left outside the core or has been brought by iron asteroids from the core of fragmented proto planets. Gold makes up about 3 parts per billion in the crust, but about 2 parts per million in the core.

Question: What is the evidence for and against the claim that increases in carbon dioxide (CO2) cause an increase in temperature, and not vice versa?
Answer: The evidence is of two different kinds. Firstly, is the direct spectroscopic analysis of the incoming energy from the sun and the outgoing energy from the Earth. If the incoming energy at the Earth’s surface is more than the outgoing energy, then the planet will heat up. This is happening now. Incoming energy is estimated at average of 340 watts per square meter. Outgoing energy is estimated at 338.4 watts per square meter - 1.6 watts less. The difference is quite small, but the excess energy accumulates. Although the energy received, and energy emitted are quite similar, they are very different in quality. The energy received is from the sun, whose surface temperature is 5525 degrees Kelvin. The spectrum is shown below. The chart shows two lines, the spectrum at the top of the atmosphere and the spectrum at ground level. The energy from the sun is mostly in the form of ultraviolet, visible and near infrared light. As it passes through the atmosphere some of the radiation energy is absorbed by atmospheric gasses. An atom of one of these gasses can absorb a unit of radiation which causes it to jump to a higher energy level. Eventually the atom returns to its base level and re-emits the energy as radiation. The radiation is emitted in all direction, so some continues to the ground, but some heads back out to space. The net result is a lesser amount of energy reaching the ground. On a clear day, with sun at the zenith, each square meter of the atmosphere receives 1361 watts, but only 1120 watts makes it down to the ground. The Earth’s average temperature is only around 285 degrees K and the spectrum of the emitted radiation reflects this temperature. Unlike the sun, the Earth’s temperature varies, so the spectrum from different parts of the Earth are different. Putting the two spectrums together shows just how different the two are. The atmosphere absorbs far more of the outgoing radiation than the incoming radiation. But remember that the outgoing must match the incoming if the Earth’s temperature is to stay constant. If the balance is disturbed then the Earth’s temperature will change to maintain the balance. The extra radiation absorbing gasses emitted by humans has created a disturbance, and the Earth’s temperature is rising and will continue to rise until outgoing radiation matches the energy of incoming radiation. Above is the theoretical evidence that increased carbon dioxide. The second line of evidence is that carbon dioxide levels (and methane levels) have risen and that temperatures have risen. Both are well documented. Also well documented is the fact that sea levels are rising as a result of increasing water temperature and melting ice. The tidal gauges for the Brisbane river mouth, close to my home, show clear evidence of a slow and steady rise.

Question: What is the most abundant gas in Earth's atmosphere by volume, and what percentage of the atmosphere does it make up?

Question: What is the scientific explanation for how life started on Earth? If there is no scientific explanation, what are some theories?
Answer: Life on Earth started a long time ago, so there is not much evidence left of exactly how it started. This is in sharp contrast to the evidence for biological evolution, which is still continuing and going on all around us. However, we can gain some clues from the evidence that we have. A clue that does come to us from the early days of the Earth is that life started relatively early. The earliest fossils date from 3.7 billion years ago - just 800 million years after the formation of the Earth. And during most of those 800 million years the environment would have been extremely hostile, with high temperatures, volcanic eruptions and bombardment by asteroids. By contrast it took another 3 billion years for multi-cellular life to appear. This suggests that single cell life can appear relatively easily. Another clue that came to light in 1952 was the famous Miller-Urey experiment that showed that amino acids - the building blocks for proteins - could be formed by lightening acting on the early Earth atmosphere. This suggests the “biotic soup” theory first articulated by Charles Darwin himself in a letter to James Hooker. "But if (and oh what a big if) we could conceive in some warm little pond with all sorts of ammonia and phosphoric salts, light, heat, electricity etcetera present, that a protein compound was chemically formed, ready to undergo still more complex changes [..] " However the search for exactly how complex life arose on Earth involves much more than biochemistry. Question: Why isn't the ground level zero on the globe located at sea-level if Earth's surface is mostly water?
Answer: With the advent of GPS, the reference point for global elevations is now the geoid, rather than the traditional benchmark - sea level. Sea level was a useful concept for comparing elevations around the world. However, it suffered from a number of distortions: The geoid is the surface that a global ocean of water with a constant density would have in the absence of wind. The geoid is a theoretical model and is highly complicated. The standard co-ordinate system used by the GPS system is known as WGS84 and is a mathematical approximation of the geoid. The co-ordinate system is based on the centre of the Earth. It is estimated that the error is less than 2 centimeters. Different countries adopt their own co-ordinate system. In Australia we use the Australian Height Datum (AHD). There is about a 1.5 meter tilt to the AHD resulting from the difference in sea temperatures from north to south and other factors. Wikipedia has good, detailed articles on the Geoid, WGS84 and the AHD.

Question: What makes it difficult to see Earth’s core?
Answer: The intervening rock makes it impossible to see the core with the visible light which our eyes are sensitive to. But other energy waves that can pass through solid rock, make it possible to examine the core in considerable detail. In particular seismic waves have given quite a detailed picture of the core. The difficulty has been in establishing seismic stations around the world and combining their data to create a coherent picture. With many years of experience, the difficulties have been overcome and much detail has been resolved. Of particular importance is the fact that seismic waves come in several different types. The two most important are pressure (P) waves and shear (S) waves. P waves are like sound waves in air - the particles vibrate in the direction of travel. S waves are like light waves, the particles vibrate at right angles to the direction of travel. The importance of this is that P waves can travel through liquids, but S waves cannot. This led to the discovery that the inner core is solid, but the outer core is liquid.

Question: What are the different forms of carbon? Why can't we find any other form of carbon on Earth?
Answer: Different crystalline forms of an element or compound are called allotropes. Carbon has many known allotropes that are present or can be created on Earth. In theory carbon has about 500 allotropes some of which require conditions not available on Earth. Some are only formed under very high pressure. For example, it is believed on theoretical grounds that at ultrahigh pressures above 145 million psi (1,000 GPa), diamond will transform into a body-centered cubic form. Such pressures are present in the core of giant planets like Neptune, but not on Earth. Some of the allotropes of carbon are: Diamond. The crystal structure of diamond is a face-centered cubic lattice having eight atoms per unit cell to form a diamond cubic structure. Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four other carbons in a tetrahedral geometry. Graphite In graphite each carbon atom is strongly attached to three others forming layers. The bonds between layers are much longer and weaker. Graphene Graphene is a single layer of graphite. It has extraordinary electrical, thermal, and physical properties. It can be produced by epitaxy on an insulating or conducting substrate or by mechanical exfoliation (repeated peeling) from graphite. Bi-graphene - two layers - has different properties again. Amorphous Carbon This is carbon that has no crystal structure. Buckminsterfullerene Buckminsterfullerenes were discovered in 1985 and are relatively large balls of carbon with a geodesic structure. Carbon Nanotubes Carbon nanotubes, also called buckytubes, are cylindrical carbon molecules. Carbon Nanofoams Carbon nanofoam consists of a cluster-assembly of carbon atoms strung together in a loose three-dimensional web. Each cluster is about 6 nanometers wide and consists of about 4000 carbon atoms linked in graphite-like sheets that are given negative curvature by the inclusion of heptagons among the regular hexagonal pattern. This is the opposite of what happens in the case of buckminsterfullerenes in which carbon sheets are given positive curvature by the inclusion of pentagons. Question: What are the parts per million of gas in our atmosphere?
Answer: Minor gasses in the atmosphere are usually expressed on a volume basis of dry air in parts per million. Thus the latest figure for carbon dioxide measured at the laboratory on Mauna Loa in Hawaii is quoted 421 parts per million. This means that after they removed all the water vapour, the laboratory found 421 molecules of carbon dioxide in every million molecules of air. Water is excluded because it is very variable, ranging from zero up to 30,000 parts per million. The major gasses (nitrogen, oxygen and argon) are often expressed in percent. Thus oxygen is often said to make up 21% of the atmosphere - which is 210,000 parts per million. Some gasses are heavier than others, hence the composition of the atmosphere by mass is different than the composition by volume. Thus carbon dioxide with a molecular weight of 44 versus the atmosphere average of 29, makes up 421 parts per million by volume but 640 perts per million by mass. In a dry air sample of 1 million pounds, the mass of carbon dioxide is 640 pounds. The various gasses composing the atmosphere are shown below. There are other trace gasses, like ozone, sulfur dioxide, radon and nitrogen oxides, but they are very minor, except where there is significant air pollution.

Question: How does the increased pressure of the ocean the deeper one goes effect objects that are falling through it? For instance, if I drop a rock from the oceans surface, will the rock slow down the deeper it goes because the water increases in density?
Answer: The density of water increases with pressure but only slightly. Density also increases as the temperature drops, and the deep oceans are cold. The following graph shows how the density of water varies with pressure and density. Let us suppose you drop a rock with a volume of 1 cubic meter and a mass of 2,700 kilograms (a big rock!) into the ocean where the surface temperature is 21 degrees C. Pure water at this temperature and pressure would have a density of 998 kilograms per cubic metre. But this is salt water, which increases the density to 1,001 kilograms per cubic metre. The net force acting on the rock will be 2,700 - 1,001 = 1,699 kilograms. At a depth of 2,000 metres, the pressure is around 200 bar, and the temperature is around 5 degrees C. The density of pure water would be about 1,009 kilograms per cubic metre. The salt would increase this to 1,012 Kilograms per cubic metre. The net force on the rock would be 2,700 - 1012 = 1,688 Kilograms - a reduction of 0.6%. However this assumes that the rock itself does not contract under the temperature fall and pressure. It probably will - more than offsetting the water density effect. A further complication is that the viscosity of water drops with pressure, but rises with decreasing temperature. Overall the viscosity will drop. A further complication is that the rock will likely absorb water as the pressure increases. This will increase its mass. The speed at which the rock drops is a function of the net force on it and the resistance of the water. It With the viscosity of the water dropping, it is likely that the speed of the falling rock will likely increase with depth.

Question: How much does "sea level" deviate around the world from a perfect sphere (due to variation in the force of gravity)?
Answer: The modern equivalent of “sea level” is the geoid. The geoid is the theoretical shape the oceans would take if they covered the Earth and the water was all at the same temperature and salinity (and hence density), and there were no tides or wind.. The major deviation of the geoid from a perfect sphere is caused by the Earth’s rotation. Centrifugal force partly offsets gravity and is much greater at the equator than towards the poles. The geoid has a polar radius of 6,356,752 meters and an equatorial radius of 6,378,137 meters - 21,385 meters greater. According to http://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/earthfact.htm the volumetric radius of the Earth is 6,371,000 meters. Thus the geoid at the equator is 7,137 meters above a perfect sphere and at the poles the geoid is 13,248 below a perfect sphere. If the Earth was perfectly uniform, the geoid would form an ellipse. However the material in the Earth varies in density, which causes the geoid to differ from the theoretical ellipsoid. Compared to the rotation of the Earth the variations due to density are quite small. The difference of the geoid ranges from 85 meters above the ellipsoid in Iceland to 106 meters below the geoid in southern India. Actual sea level also differs from the geoid due to differences in the density of the water, due to temperature or salinity. These variations are smaller again at less than half a meter.

Question: When was the average thickness of the Earth's crust first calculated or estimated? What did scientists know about the thickness of the Earth's crust before the 20th century? In what interval(s) fell their measurements?

The first practical seismograph for measuring seismic waves from earthquakes was developed in Japan in the 1880s by a team of John Milne, James Ewing and Thomas Grey. During the 1890s and 1900s seismic stations were set up in different locations. Precise timing of the arrival of waves from particular earthquakes allowed a knowledge of the structure of the Earth to slowly develop. In 1897 Richard Oldham distinguished between P (pressure) waves and S (shear) waves which travel at different speeds through solid rock. S waves cannot travel at all through liquids. The Croatian geophysicist Andrija Mohorovičić analysed the arrival of seismic waves from the October 8th 1909 Kupa Valley earthquake in the Pokuplje region of Croatia. He noted the timing of the S and P waves from the event and postulated a discontinuity below the surface where the speed of the waves suddenly changed. This layer is now known as the Mohorovičić discontinuity and marks the boundary between the crust and the underlying mantle. He estimated the depth at 54 kilometers. According to the paper continental crust is 20 to 80 kilometres thick, whereas ocean crust is much thinner at 6 to 10 kilometres. Richard Oldham had suggested a liquid core based on the shadow of S waves from events on the other side of the globe. Beno Gutenberg in 1914 confirmed the suggestion and accurately established the depth of the solid/liquid transition at 2,880 kilometres.

Question: What is going on with Earth's inner core? Spinning, stopping, reversing? What effects will this cause?
Answer: Since 1936 it has been known that the inner core of the Earth is solid and the outer core liquid. The evidence for this is from seismic rays generated by earthquakes, nuclear tests and blasting. Seismic waves are of two basic types - P or pressure waves where the vibration is in line with the direction of travel and S or shear waves where the vibration is at right angles to the direction of travel. P waves can pass through liquids, but S waves only pass through solids. By measuring exact arrival times of the different waves at seismic stations around the world, the structure of the Earth can be determined. Because the outer core is liquid it is possible that the inner core is rotating at a different speed to the mantle and crust of the Earth. In 1975, it was suggested that differential rotation of the inner core could account for the westward drift of the Earth’s north magnetic pole. It was estimated that the difference was about 3 degrees per year. This would mean that the inner core would complete one complete rotation relative to the mantle and crust every 120 years. In 1995, detailed analysis of seismic waves suggested that the core is rotating faster than the mantle and crust by about 1 degree per year - meaning a complete rotation every 360 years. Then just recently in January 2023, Yi Yang and Xiaodong Song have published a paper in Nature Geoscience Multidecadal variation of the Earth’s inner-core rotation that claims that the differential rotation is cyclic and swings back and forth from faster than the mantle to slower than the mantle with a period of 70 years. Right now according to the authors we are in mid cycle and the differential rotation is close to zero. The paper is available from Nature Geoscience, and a less technical explanation is available at Earth's Inner Core May Right Now Be in The Process of Changing Direction Two of the figures from the Nature article are shown below: As you can see, the evidence is very subtle. The slow differential rotation is unlikely to have much effect on the surface, apart from possibly the movement of the Earth’s magnetic axis.

For example, when blue green algae first evolved in the oceans about 2 billion years ago, they used photosynthesis to produce elemental oxygen. The oxygen turned soluble ferrous ions in the ocean into non-soluble ferric ions which precipitated out and formed the massive iron ore beds running 50–65% iron that form the basis of our steel industry. Or for another example hot liquids circulating close to volcanic rocks have dissolved metals which then precipitate out when conditions change to form the massive porphyry deposits from which most of our gold and copper is mined. None of these processes are active in the mantle, which undergoes a slow convective churning, mixing the elements so that none form economically attractive concentrations. The interactions between the mantle and the crust already concentrate some elements - as recorded in the table below. As per the table the concentration of copper (Cu) in the mantle is estimated at 20 parts per million. Due to interactions between the mantle and the crust, the concentration rises to 75 parts per million in the crust. From there hydrothermal and other processes have produced the concentrations of 10,000 parts per million or more which constitute an economically mineable deposit. Furthermore, even if there were economic concentrations of minerals in the mantle, we could never reach them. Our deepest mine goes down 4 kilometers. The deepest drill hole gets to 12 kilometers - far short of the 70 kilometers needed to reach the mantle.

Question: Why did I just read from Washington post that Earth’s inner core seems to be slowing its spin?
Answer: Knowledge of the nature of the inner parts of the Earth is gleaned from various sources, some rather speculative. The density of the Earth shows that it can’t be all rock - there must be something denser. The most common denser element found in meteorites is iron, so the assumption is that the dense core of the Earth consists of iron, along with associated other elements. Another clue is given by the study of seismic waves. These waves are generated by earthquakes, nuclear tests and even mine blasting. There are numerous seismic stations around the world. Valuable information is generate by the precise timing at which waves from a particular event arrive at different stations. There are several different kinds of waves. The most important are P (pressure) waves and S (shear) waves. In P waves particles vibrate in the direction of travel . Sound is a P wave. S waves vibrate at right angles to the direction of travel. Light is an S wave. (Ocean waves are surface waves - a third form. Much earthquake damage results from surface waves but they are less important for seismology). The important difference between S and P waves is that P waves can transmit through liquids, but S waves are limited to solids. This is how seismologists first found that the core of the Earth is liquid. In 1936 the Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann used more sophisticated analysis to show that the inner core of the Earth is solid. Seismologists usually call layers where there are abrupt changes in seismic behaviour ‘discontinuities’. By rights the boundary between the inner solid and outer liquid core should have been named after Inge as the Lehmann discontinuity. However there was already another discontinuity named after her, so it’s usually called the Bullen discontinuity. Reproducing the conditions at the centre of the Earth in the laboratory is very hard. There is some support for the idea that the solid core is crystalline pure iron. Latent heat released by the solidification of iron under high pressure would make the Bullen discontinuity very hot. In 1996 further more sophisticated analysis of how arrival times of seismic waves had changed over the years caused Geophysicist Paul Richards of Columbia University to propose that the solid core is rotating slightly faster than the outer parts of the planet. The difference in speed is tiny - about 1 degree per year. (Note the Earth rotates 365 x 360 = 131,400 degrees in a year.) Now geophysicists Xiaodong Song of Peking University in Beijing and Paul Richards of the Lamont Doherty Earth Observatory in New York have published a paper that proposes that the inner core rotation has slowed slightly and is falling behind that of the rest of the planet. They propose an oscillation over a 70 year time period. Once again the difference in rotation speeds is tiny. You can read their results and conclusions in their paper at or in somewhat less technical form in newspapers like the Post and New York Times, or in Science News - Earth’s inner core may be reversing its rotation A diagram from Song and Richard’s paper is shown below.

Question: What is the closest volcano to Great Britain and Ireland? Why aren't volcanoes more common on this island chain?
Answer: There are volcanoes in the British Isles but they are all extinct, having mostly erupted hundreds of millions of years ago. Volcanoes form at plate boundaries (Iceland, Andes, New Zealand), or over hot spots in the mantle (Hawaii). The British Isles are now not close to a plate boundary or over a hot spot. When the North American Plate split from the Eurasian Plate in the Triassic period some 250 million years ago, what is now the British Isles was close to the edge of the Eurasian plate. However, as the Atlantic has widened, the seafloor spreading has moved the British Isles further and further away from the active divergence. Some activities did remain, possibly on hot spots. One of the most recent volcanoes in the British Isles was at the Cuillin on the Isle of Skye. It is the remnants of volcanic activity from about 60 million years ago. Arthur’s Seat in Edinburgh is much older - about 340 million years ago.
